text: In November 1783, the last British ships and troops left New York City,and American troops marched in. As Washington said good-bye to hisofficers in a New York tavern, he hugged each one. Tears ran down hisface. He became so upset that he had to leave the room.Earlier in the fall, Washington had written a farewell letter to hisarmies. In it, he praised them by saying that their endurance “throughalmost every possible suffering and discouragement for the space of eightlong years, was little short of a standing miracle.”By their persistence, the Americans won independence even thoughthey faced many obstacles. As you have read, they lacked training andexperience. They were often short of supplies and weapons. By contrast,the British forces ranked among the best trained in the world. They were

experienced and well-supplied professional soldiers. Yet the Americanshad certain advantages that enabled them to win. British generals were overconfident and madepoor decisions. By contrast, Washington learned from his mistakes.After early defeats, he developed the strategy of dragging out thewar to wear down the British. Despite difficulties, he never gave up. Britain’s rivals, especially France, helped America.Foreign loans and military aid were essential to America’s victory. The Americans knew the land where thewar took place and used that knowledge well.The British could con-trol coastal cities but could not extend their control to the interior. The Americans had more reason to fight. At stake werenot only their lives but also their property and their dream of liberty.
citation: García, Jesús, Donna M. Ogle, C. Frederick Risinger, and Joyce Stevos. Creating America, Grades 6–8: Beginnings Through World War I. McDougal Littell/Houghton Mifflin, 2003.
title: Creating America, Grades 6–8: Beginnings Through World War I
